etymology.text: From Middle High German hūs, from Old High German hūs, from Proto-West Germanic *hūs, from Proto-Germanic *hūsą. Cognate with Old Frisian hūs, Low German Hus, Huus, Dutch huis, Icelandic hús, Danish hus, Swedish hus, English house.

funFacts: The Bauhaus (1919), the famous school of design, means “building house”.
Haus and English house were the same word a thousand years ago: Old High German and Old English both said hūs.
pitfalls: Plural with umlaut: das Haus – die Häuser (dative den Häusern).
At home = zu Hause, (going) home = nach Hause – both keep an old dative -e (Austria and Switzerland also write zuhause).
subtleties: Haus is a building; your home as a feeling is das Zuhause or das Heim.
Dative dem Haus or (older, set phrases) dem Hause.

etymology.text: From Middle High German wonunge, from Old High German wonunga, from Proto-West Germanic *wunungu, equivalent to wohnen + -ung. Related to Dutch woning (“house, residence”).

funFacts: Wohnung is wohnen (to live, dwell) + -ung; the same pattern makes the noun from many verbs: rechnen → Rechnung.
pitfalls: A Wohnung is a flat; a whole building for one family is a Haus.
Every noun in -ung is feminine: die Wohnung, die Zeitung, die Rechnung.
subtleties: A Dreizimmerwohnung counts the living room and bedrooms – kitchen and bathroom are not counted.
Germany has one of the lowest home-ownership rates in the EU – about half of households rent – so Wohnung and Miete (rent) are everyday words.

profile.feeling: A cup of coffee or tea, a break, a chat.

senses.def: cup (with a handle, for hot drinks), mug

examples.text: Möchtest du eine Tasse Kaffee?
examples.tr: Would you like a cup of coffee?

examples.text: Die Tasse ist leer.
examples.tr: The cup is empty.

examples.text: Die Tassen stehen im Schrank.
examples.tr: The cups are in the cupboard.

phrases.text: nicht alle Tassen im Schrank haben
phrases.tr: not to have all the cups in the cupboard
phrases.meaning: to be crazy

phrases.tr: Cups up!
phrases.meaning: cheers! (raise your glasses)

synonyms.nuance: mug, beaker – no saucer; also a paper cup (Kaffeebecher)

etymology.text: From Late Middle High German *tasse, from Middle French tasse, from Arabic طَاس (ṭās), variant of طَسْت (ṭast), from Middle Persian tšt’ (tašt). Cognate with Modern French tasse, Dutch tas.

funFacts: Tasse came from Arabic طَاس (ṭās, a bowl) through French – the Arabic word is also behind Turkish tas (bowl).
pitfalls: No “of”: eine Tasse Kaffee (a cup of coffee), zwei Tassen Tee.
die Tasse (cup) ≠ die Tasche (bag).
subtleties: A Becher is a mug without a saucer; Tasse is the classic cup, often with a saucer (Untertasse).

plurals.note: as a measure after a number: zwei Glas Wein, drei Glas Honig

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

senseForms.note: the material: no plural, often without an article (aus Glas)

profile.feeling: Drinking glasses, jars, the material – and a toast.

examples.text: Ein Glas Wasser, bitte.
examples.tr: A glass of water, please.

examples.text: Die Gläser sind im Schrank.
examples.tr: The glasses are in the cupboard.

examples.text: Die Flasche ist aus Glas.
examples.tr: The bottle is made of glass.

examples.text: Ich kaufe ein Glas Honig.
examples.tr: I’m buying a jar of honey.

phrases.text: zu tief ins Glas geschaut haben
phrases.tr: to have looked too deep into the glass
phrases.meaning: to have drunk too much

phrases.text: Wer im Glashaus sitzt, sollte nicht mit Steinen werfen.
phrases.tr: Who sits in a glass house should not throw stones.
phrases.meaning: don’t criticise others for faults you have yourself

synonyms.nuance: beaker, tumbler without a stem; plastic cup

etymology.text: From Old High German glas, gles, from Proto-West Germanic *glas, from Proto-Germanic *glasą, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰel- (“to shine, glimmer, glow”). Compare Low German Glas, Dutch glas, English glass.

funFacts: Glas comes from a root meaning “to shine” – a fitting origin for glass.
pitfalls: Plural with umlaut: die Gläser. But after a number, as a measure: zwei Glas Bier (two glasses of beer).
Glasses for the eyes are a Brille, not Gläser.
subtleties: ein Glas Wasser – no “of”, like eine Tasse Kaffee.

homonyms.none: no other noun with this form

senseForms.none: one meaning

profile.feeling: Meals: a full plate, an empty plate, a plate of soup.

examples.text: Stell bitte die Teller auf den Tisch.
examples.tr: Please put the plates on the table.

examples.text: Der Teller ist leer.
examples.tr: The plate is empty.

examples.text: Ich esse einen Teller Suppe.
examples.tr: I’m having a plate of soup.

phrases.tr: to look over the rim of the plate
phrases.meaning: to think outside the box, look beyond one’s own field

etymology.text: From Middle High German teller (“plate”), from Middle French tailloir (“plate, cutting board”).

funFacts: Teller comes from French tailloir, from tailler “to cut”: a medieval plate was a board to cut meat on.
pitfalls: English teller (bank clerk) is a false friend.
Plural = singular: die Teller (dative den Tellern).
subtleties: ein Teller Suppe – no “of”, like eine Tasse Kaffee.
